title: Trump's $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee Blocked Again as Appeals Court Denies Stay
excerpt: The First Circuit's July 24 ruling means the controversial fee — which had chilled H-1B applications to just 85 payments — is no longer in effect, though the administration vows to fight on.
body:
• The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied the government's request to keep the $100,000 H-1B fee in place while it appeals a lower court ruling that struck it down as an unlawful tax.
  • The fee, imposed by presidential proclamation in September 2025, reduced H-1B applications to a trickle — only 85 payments were made by February 2026.
  • Nearly three-quarters of H-1B visa approvals go to Indian workers, making this one of the most consequential immigration policies for the Indian diaspora.
  • The administration says it will comply but "strongly disagrees" and may pursue further legal action, with the case likely headed to the Supreme Court.

The $100,000 fee that President Donald Trump imposed on new H-1B visa applications is no longer in effect after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied the government's motion for a stay on July 24, according to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

The Department of Homeland Security said it "strongly disagrees with the First Circuit's order denying the stay request but will comply with the court's order" while considering next steps. DHS added that if the order is later lifted, it still plans to collect the payment.

The ruling marks the latest chapter in a sprawling legal battle over Trump's September 2025 proclamation, which raised the cost of obtaining an H-1B visa from roughly $2,000–$5,000 to $100,000 — a 20-to-50-fold increase that sent shockwaves through the tech industry, universities, and hospitals that rely on skilled foreign workers.

From Proclamation to Courtroom

Trump signed Presidential Proclamation 10973 on September 19, 2025, imposing the $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions filed for workers located outside the United States who would need consular processing. The fee took effect two days later. Workers already in the U.S. on student visas — who make up a large share of new H-1B recipients — were exempted.

The administration framed the fee as a tool to protect American workers.

"The effect is to incentivize companies to train up and hire American workers."

— Tiberius Davis, U.S. Department of Justice lawyer

The response from employers was swift and dramatic. By February 15, 2026, USCIS had received just 85 payments of the fee — a stark indicator of how effectively the cost increase had discouraged participation in the H-1B program, which offers 65,000 visas annually plus 20,000 for workers with advanced degrees.

The fee triggered at least three major lawsuits. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, representing 300,000 businesses, filed suit in Washington, D.C., calling it the group's first legal challenge against the Trump administration. A coalition of 20 Democratic state attorneys general brought a case in Boston. And a group of religious organizations and labor unions sued in San Francisco.

Competing Court Rulings

The legal battles produced contradictory outcomes. In December 2025, U.S. District Judge Beryl Howell in Washington sided with the government, ruling that the fee fell within the president's broad immigration powers. The Chamber of Commerce appealed.

But on June 8, 2026, U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin in Boston reached the opposite conclusion. In a 42-page decision, Sorokin ruled that the $100,000 charge was not a lawful immigration penalty but an unauthorized tax that Congress never approved.

"The substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called."

— Judge Leo Sorokin, U.S. District Court, Boston

Sorokin cited the Supreme Court's February 2026 ruling striking down Trump's sweeping tariffs, reasoning that the same legal logic applied: the president cannot levy a tax without congressional authorization. The court also found the fee violated the Administrative Procedure Act by bypassing required notice-and-comment rulemaking.

The administration appealed within days and temporarily won a stay of Sorokin's order. But the First Circuit's July 24 denial of a continued stay means the fee is once again vacated nationwide.

Deep Impact on Indian Workers

Indians are the largest group of H-1B visa recipients, accounting for nearly three-quarters of all approvals, according to NPR. The $100,000 fee hit the Indian diaspora community particularly hard, with states arguing that filling vacancies for doctors and teachers through the program was already difficult before the increase.

Indian diaspora organizations welcomed the courts' intervention. "We welcome the Massachusetts federal court's decision striking down the $100,000 H-1B visa fee, which restores predictability and fairness to the employment-based immigration system," Khanderao Kand, Chief of Policy and Strategy at the Foundation for India and Indian Diaspora Studies (FIIDS), told PTI.

Sanjeev Joshipura, Executive Director of Indiaspora, struck a more cautious note, warning that the administration could still create procedural obstacles for H-1B holders even if the fee is permanently struck down. "All stakeholders connected with H-1B visas will heave a sigh of relief after the court order, but one wonders if this is truly the end of the matter," he told PTI.

What's Next

The legal fight is far from over. With conflicting rulings from federal judges in Boston and Washington — and a third case pending in San Francisco — the dispute is likely headed to the Supreme Court.

The original proclamation was set to expire in September 2026, but the administration has shown no signs of backing down. White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said the administration is "confident" that the Boston ruling will be reversed on appeal.

For now, employers and H-1B workers have a reprieve. New H-1B petitions requiring consular processing no longer require the $100,000 payment. But immigration attorneys are advising clients to act quickly, given the possibility that the fee could be reinstated without notice if a higher court sides with the government.
nri_angle: Nearly three-quarters of H-1B approvals go to Indian workers; the $100,000 fee had severely curtailed applications, and Indian diaspora groups have welcomed the court rulings blocking it.
author: Diaspora Desk
